Trump Questions Whether US Midterm Elections Were 'Honest' as He Casts Doubt on Voting Machines After Democratic Wins
From congratulations to suspicion, Trump's response to the Republican defeat takes a different turn
Donald Trump questioned whether the US midterm elections were 'honest' on Monday, casting suspicion on voting machines and large early-voting totals without presenting evidence of wrongdoing. His remarks marked a shift from his initial response to Democratic victories that are set to give the party control of both chambers of Congress when the new session begins in January 2027.
'Does anybody really believe that this "Election" was honest,' the president wrote on Truth Social, asking: 'How could the Polls be so wrong???' He added: 'It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!'
Trump Questions Voting Machines and Early Ballots
Trump claimed some early voting 'dumps' were so large that it was 'impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote'. He did not identify a particular equipment failure or provide evidence that ballots had been incorrectly counted.
His comments followed Democratic victories in Republican strongholds as well as competitive races, with the party outperforming several pre-election forecasts. Rather than identifying a documented discrepancy, the post presented the size of the Democratic victory as a reason to question the voting process.
Georgia and Texas Figures Show Democratic Leads
In Georgia, Jon Ossoff received 1,771,988 early and mail-in votes, exceeding Republican Mike Collins's reported overall total after Election Day by 60,352. The comparison used all votes recorded for Collins at that point, not simply those cast for him on Election Day itself.
In Texas, James Talarico received 4,397,474 early votes against Republican Ken Paxton's reported overall tally of 4,249,373, a difference of 148,101. Those Texas figures came from state election data last updated late on Thursday afternoon, making them a dated count rather than certified final returns.
North Carolina Comparison Excludes Mail Ballots
Roy Cooper's early in-person votes in North Carolina also exceeded the overall total recorded for Republican Michael Whatley, even without including mail ballots on Cooper's side. That differs from the Georgia comparison, which combined Ossoff's early and mail-in votes before measuring them against Collins's total across voting methods.
Together, the three comparisons illustrate the scale of Democratic voting before Election Day, although they use different ballot categories and figures available at the time. They do not establish that voting machines affected the results or explain, by themselves, why the candidates won.
Pew Finds Polls Underestimated Democratic Margins
Pew Research Center's preliminary assessment compared pre-election polling averages with unofficial results available on 4 November in 27 Senate and gubernatorial races. Published on 6 November, it found that polls understated Democratic margins by at least two percentage points in 23 contests, with a mean underestimate of about four percentage points across all 27.
The analysis found that polling captured the election's broad direction but missed the size of the Democratic advantage, while also identifying greater enthusiasm among Democratic supporters. They were more likely to participate in pre-election surveys, although Pew said further research was needed to establish the causes of the polling errors.
Trump Initially Congratulated Democratic Winners
Trump initially congratulated Democratic winners before questioning election integrity on Monday. His earlier response included praise for their campaign performance: 'Congratulations to the Democrats, they did a good job.'
His latest remarks shifted attention from the Republican defeat to the voting process, without identifying a specific irregularity that would substantiate his machine-related suspicions. Once the new Congress takes office, Democrats' majorities will leave Trump pursuing his legislative agenda with an opposition-controlled House and Senate for the remaining two years of his presidency.

'Not Honest': Trump questions 2026 midterm integrity and claims results are biased after GOP losses
United States President Donald Trumpu analyzing the heavy political fallout from historic congressional defeats as fresh economic pressures and deep polarization reshape Washington
Following the Republican Party's major defeats in the 2026 midterm elections, United States President Donald Trump questioned the integrity and accuracy of the results, taking to social media to cast doubt on the outcome.
As reported, Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump questioned how pre-election polling could have been so misaligned with the final results and openly raised doubts about whether the election was "honest".
These remarks arrived after historic midterm outcomes where Democrats flipped control of Congress.
While figures within his own party and independent analysts pointed to factors like economic frustrations, surging costs, and the administration's foreign policy choices (such as the war in Iran) as the driving forces behind the GOP losses, Trump's statements echoed familiar skepticism regarding election processes.
This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.
Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.
In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing.
The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
"We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported," he said.
Stewart added that in some states, like Florida and Georgia, some initial reporting of results happens quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots.
Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
As reported by BBC, surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi.
Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.
Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.

What the Texas returns show
In Texas, state Rep. James Talarico (D-Austin) won the U.S. Senate race, and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D-Austin) defeated Gov. Greg Abbott (R-Texas), as The Dallas Express reported on election night.
A breakdown of Texas Secretary of State data showed Talarico with 4,397,474 votes in the early-vote tally, about 148,000 more than Attorney General Ken Paxton (R-Texas) received overall. Talarico also led Paxton by 30,802 votes on Election Day.
A November 1 New York Times/Siena poll put Talarico ahead by seven percentage points and Hinojosa ahead by one. The state’s unofficial returns put their leads at about 12 and seven points, respectively.
Tarrant County’s count
Tarrant County scheduled its first election-night release for 7:15 p.m. or earlier. That report covered 582,119 early in-person and absentee ballots, about 79% of the 733,287 ballots in its November 4 update.
The county’s preliminary reconciliation put the ballot count 1,016 above the adjusted voter count, a gap of 0.14%. The adjustment subtracts rejected or pending ballots from the voter tally. The report said staff were checking variances in mail, early in-person and Election Day voting.
Tarrant County planned to resume counting ballots no earlier than 5 p.m. Monday. As of Monday afternoon, the county had yet to post its final reconciliation or hand-count audit results.

Trump Questions Midterm Election Results as He Raises Fresh Claims of Voting Machine Fraud: 'How Could the Polls Be So Wrong?'
Nov. 9 2026, Published 4:26 p.m. ET
Donald Trump has returned to his election fraud allegations with a blistering attack on Democrats, RadarOnline.com can report.
Days after congratulating Democrats for doing a "good job" in their midterm election victory, which saw them retake control of both chambers of Congress, Trump appeared to do an about-face on the results.
Donald Trump Questions the Midterm Election Results
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest,' he asked in a Truth Social post shared on Monday, November 9.
"How could the Polls be so wrong???" he continued. "Some early voting 'dumps' were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote."
The 80-year-old ended his rant by revisiting his accusations that the computerized vote counters may be faulty and untrustworthy.
"It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!" he exclaimed.
Trump Previously Promised to Work with Democrats
Trump is no stranger to suggesting potential voter fraud after GOP defeats in elections, but things felt surprisingly different this year, when he seemed to take a more conciliatory tone after the Democratic drubbing.
On Election Night, Trump told The New York Times that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results of the midterms.
"We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them," Trump told the outlet. "We’ll probably work something out."
Trump then gave his enemies credit for their performance, saying: "I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. They fought hard."
Democratic Leaders Challenge the President's Accusations
While the president returned to bashing the "Dumocrats" online, the incoming majority continued to take its victory lap, with Democratic Senator Chuck Schumer clapping back at Trump's tantrum.
"Donald Trump's pathetic return to election denialism was inevitable," Schumer, 75, shared on X. "He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure."
Just days before the election, Trump touted a $1million reward for anyone who reports voter fraud in the November midterms, provided the tip leads to an arrest and conviction.
He did not, however, explain how the reward would be funded, how people should submit tips, or who would determine whether a report qualified for payment.
President Trump's History of Voter Fraud Allegations
Still, Trump has returned time and again to his unsubstantiated voter fraud theories. During a July 16 speech on election security, Trump revived claims about vulnerabilities and alleged problems with the 2020 election that experts said had already been debunked.
His administration subsequently released records containing sensitive information states had shared with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), including logs of communications and activity monitored on Election Day 2020.
However, the disclosure might have backfired. Former CISA officials said the release undermined the trust necessary for states to share sensitive cybersecurity information with the federal government.
One former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official who now advises state governments said some officials were unlikely to share information with CISA again.

sources.news_title: Trump revives election fraud claims after crushing midterm defeat
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday revived baseless allegations of election fraud, reversing his initial acceptance of last week’s midterm results after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in a crushing defeat for his Republican Party.
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, offering no evidence of wrongdoing.
“Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” he added.
“It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”
The extraordinary reversal came six days after Americans delivered a sweeping rejection of Trump’s party, handing Democrats their biggest House majority in nearly two decades and control of the Senate.
Trump initially struck an unusually conciliatory tone, congratulating his opponents and acknowledging they had fought a successful campaign.
“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he told The New York Times on election night, adding that he looked forward to working with Democrats.
He subsequently praised their campaign on Fox News, declaring: “I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do.”
But on Thursday, Trump demanded that votes cast for two minor candidates in Alaska’s still-undecided US Senate election be transferred to the trailing Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan.
“There is no other fair solution!” he insisted, despite Alaska’s election laws providing for ranked-choice voting.
Monday’s accusations went further, casting doubt on the legitimacy of the elections nationwide.
They echoed Trump’s repeated and unfounded claims that the 2020 presidential election had been stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden.
His refusal to accept that defeat sparked dozens of unsuccessful legal challenges and culminated in the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol by his supporters.
‘Election denialism’
Democrats reacted furiously to the president’s latest accusations.
“Donald Trump’s pathetic return to election denialism was inevitable,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said.
“He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure.”
Trump offered no details of the supposed irregularities, identifying neither the voting machines he questioned nor specific evidence that ballots had been improperly counted.
Pre-election polls had generally pointed toward Democratic gains, although they underestimated the scale of the party’s victories.
Election officials across the country reported largely trouble-free voting.
The Republican president had previously blamed his party’s defeat on his absence from the ballot, despite repeatedly urging supporters during the campaign to vote as though he were running himself.
He also acknowledged that the deeply unpopular war with Iran, which sent fuel prices soaring, had contributed to the losses.
The Democrats’ commanding congressional majorities will give them extensive powers to investigate his administration and obstruct his legislative agenda when the new Congress takes office in January.
Trump, however, will retain his presidential veto and considerable executive powers.

sources.news_title: Trump casts doubt on election results after saying he was ‘absolutely willing’ to accept them
sources.text:
Days after saying he was “absolutely willing” to accept the massive Republican losses in the midterm elections, President Donald Trump suggested Monday on social media that the Democratic victories weren’t “honest.”
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” he wrote on Truth Social, implying there was something nefarious about elections carried out under different processes in different states.
“It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” the post concluded, without elaborating. Election officials nationwide have reported that voting this year was largely routine.
Trump, speaking to reporters later in the day, was asked whether he thought the midterms had been rigged.
“Well, I think the numbers were terrible in terms of those early votes. You look at all those early votes,” he said, before he pivoted to talking about the still-undecided Senate race in Alaska.
A White House official, asked earlier in the day about the president’s post, noted that Trump had told reporters ahead of last week’s elections that he would respect the results “if they’re honest elections.”
In the lead-up to the election, the Justice Department sent a number of legal letters raising the specter of noncitizen voting and fraud in a number of Democratic-led states, which a judge found was an attempt to intimidate election officials.
Trump has a history of denying election results. His previous false claims include that the 2016 Iowa caucuses were rigged against him when he lost to Sen. Ted Cruz, that he won the national popular vote in 2016 despite losing it by almost 3 million votes, and that he won the 2020 election despite losing it by 7 million votes.
Yet, by the time election night arrived last week and the scale of Democrats’ victory became clear, Trump suggested he would accept the midterm results — while noting that he was not on the ballot.
“I’m absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told The New York Times in an interview Tuesday night.
“I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” he wrote that night on Truth Social.
“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he wrote in another.
In an interview with “60 Minutes” that aired Sunday, Trump ran through a number of reasons why Republicans lost, including that his deportation policies “might be too tough” and that voters “didn’t like the war. They didn’t like that gasoline was up.”
“In some cases, they didn’t like the candidates, and that’s their prerogative,” Trump said in the interview, which was taped Friday.
“I was not on the ballot, but I campaigned hard for some people, and I think if I was on the ballot, it would have been a much different situation, because you saw the level of popularity and love,” he said.
His stance seemed to start to shift Saturday, after he replaced longtime chief of staff Susie Wiles with MAGA favorite Stephen Miller.
That was the day Trump on Truth Social reposted an X user who questioned how so many states could have had their votes swing by 15% in the midterm elections.
“A pattern this even demands answers at the ballot level: paper ballot hand counts, poll-book check-ins against votes counted, and voter files showing who actually turned out,” the post said.
Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat, told NBC News that Trump’s claims about the election are “completely false.”
“The systems worked,” and “the election was a massive rebuke of his leadership,” Aguilar said in a phone interview.

Claims about a rigged election were sparse as polls opened and results came in. Most focused on casting a conspiratorial shadow on real mishaps caused by bad weather in Arizona and malfunctioning machines in Westchester County, New York. In the latter case, election officials followed established contingency plans to use backup machines and said all votes cast would be counted.
The incidents got little pickup from influential accounts, and Trump paid them little mind on his own social media channels.
Researchers at the University of Washington who were tracking false narratives on election night told reporters their early analysis shows the spread of such rumors was much smaller at the onset of the night than during elections past. Immediately following election night, those rumors died down.

sources.text:
WASHINGTON—President Donald Trump questioned the integrity of midterm election results on Nov. 9, citing polling irregularities and early vote totals as potential evidence of fraud.

Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, dropping seven Senate seats and 44 House seats so far.
Trump told reporters last week that he would accept the result after many of the races were called in Democrats’ favor.
The president has repeatedly described the 2020 election as stolen after President Joe Biden received 81.2 million votes—the most ever cast for a candidate in U.S. history—in the midst of a pandemic.
Questions of election integrity have lingered in several of the nation’s elections since the “hanging chad” situation in Florida resulted in the Supreme Court ordering that ballot counting stop in 2000, thus awarding the victory to former Texas Gov. sources.news_title: Trump Is Claiming Voter Fraud. Will the MAGA Power Structure Join In?
sources.text:
Just as day follows night and spring follows winter, one of the most inevitable occurrences in American life has begun again: Donald Trump is baselessly complaining about voter fraud following an election he did not win. After a strangely muted early reaction, a pledge to accept the results and work with Democrats, and then some furious posts on TruthSocial over the weekend, the president finally said explicitly that he doesn’t trust the election’s outcome. The fact that he would do so was never in doubt; the real question is whether other powerful people will follow suit.
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump wrote on his TruthSocial platform early Monday morning. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter! President DJT”
After so many years of collective exposure to the president’s psyche, it’s tempting to armchair psychologize and presume that this time his heart isn’t really in it. After all, he only authored one post, rather than the multi-part screed to which we’ve all become accustomed. And the posts written by other people that he shared over the weekend questioned results but stopped short of explicitly accusing anyone of fraud. “Honest question,” one read, above a somewhat illegible, blurry screenshot of a graph showing Texas voter turnout numbers, where the X-axis has been cut off. “Does anyone believe this at all? Still votes to count but… damn…”
In the leadup to the election, a great many MAGA aligned pundits and elected officials suggested that Democrats would steal the midterms, and indeed, that fraud was already in progress. In California, for instance, Bilal Essayli, a senior Trump-appointed prosecutor, claimed on X over the summer that there “is evidence of election fraud in California,” and that “more investigations are underway.” Earlier in the year, former Trump advisor Steve Bannon called for ICE to be at polling places, declaring, “We’re going to have ICE surround the polls come November. We’re not going to sit here and allow you to steal the country again. And you can whine and cry and throw your toys out of the pram all you want, but we will never again allow an election to be stolen.” Trump officials refused to rule out the idea of sending ICE or the military to polling places, even though it’s nakedly illegal.
In the end, however, ICE agents or the military didn’t show up, and no widespread allegations of voter fraud are currently being made. Trump is, in fact, strangely alone on this one; the White House X account hasn’t yet shared any fraud claims, although the account shared a post just before the election promising to investigate voting fraud. Trump’s vice president JD Vance also hasn’t engaged in the claim that fraud occurred, instead saying explicitly that the war in Iran was, as he put it, in a tweet, “the reason we lost.” No other prominent MAGA elected officials are yet making the claim either.
The lack of fraud accusations is so pronounced that Trump ally and mega-fan Laura Loomer complained over the weekend that other Republicans aren’t taking the issue seriously enough. “Have you noticed how so called ‘conservatives’ have been more focused on attacking President Trump’s inner circle as opposed to talking about the stories popping up in key states regarding suspected voter fraud?” she tweeted. “It’s one big opp. A lot of these people made deals with Democrats and you can tell they really couldn’t care less about what happens to our country so long as they get to livestream and cash in their super chats. The math isn’t making sense in Texas. That’s for sure.”
In fairness, there is one other prominent MAGA figure loudly making election fraud claims: MyPillow founder and established election-denialist Mike Lindell. This is especially bold of Lindell, given that he was sued for $1.3 billion in 2021 by Dominion Voting Systems over his claims that their machines were rigged; the parties agreed to a confidential settlement in 2026.
But even Lindell seemed to put a limit on the reach of his claims. “My cybersecurity team has identified what we believe are matching algorithmic patterns across multiple states, including Texas and Kansas,” Lindell tweeted, over a video of himself on LindellTV, the streaming platform he owns; the chyron as he spoke read, “ELECTION FRAUD IS OBVIOUS IN AMERICA.”
Lindell promised to release more information on Monday night and to show which elections, as he put it, “were taken.” It’s safe to say he’ll have at least one, very powerful, viewer.

sources.news_title: Trump has finally decided the midterms were rigged. It smacks of desperation
sources.text:
And lo, on the first morning of Stephen Miller’s service as Donald Trump’s new White House Chief of Staff, it came to pass that the US President did intend to contest the outcome of the midterm elections after all.
After spending almost a week indicating that he accepted the Democratic Party’s landslide win as fair, Trump suddenly took to his Truth Social account on Monday morning to announce that, in fact, he thinks it was rigged.
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest”, he asked, possibly rhetorically since he deployed no question mark at the end of the sentence. “How could the Polls be so wrong???” he went on to enquire.
To be fair to Trump, the final opinion polls of the midterm cycle were indeed wrong, but perhaps not in the way that he believes. Rather, they dramatically understated the scale of the Democrats’ tsunami. Some top Democratic strategists believe the party could have swept up even more victories, particularly in additional southern states, if only the polling had offered a more accurate guide to races that ended up with narrow Republican wins.
“Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote”, he claimed. That is a possible reference to the fact that in Texas, for example, Democratic senator-elect James Talarico won more votes in early voting alone than his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, secured in total.
Democrats will argue that the scale of Talarico’s win simply demonstrates the weakness of Paxton’s campaign, and the foolhardy nature of Trump’s defenestration earlier this year of John Cornyn, the state’s respected Republican senator, who may well have won re-election if his name had remained on the Texas ballot.
Trump’s intervention on Monday was once again rooted in the proven falsehood that there is a problem with the nation’s voting machines. “It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” Trump insisted. He did not explain whether he still believes – as he claimed after Joe Biden’s presidential win in 2020 – that a vast international conspiracy involving the Venezuelan government, Hungarian-born financier George Soros and the “deep state” has somehow infected America’s voting machines with compromised components.
No legal challenge mounted by Trump’s supporters has ever come up with the goods to support those conspiratorial claims. But one voting machine manufacturer – Dominion – has secured more than $854m from Fox News and Newsmax after accusing the two right-leaning TV networks of defamation following the 2020 presidential campaign.
The appetite in the United States for another protracted bout of efforts by the President to smear the electoral system is limited. Reacting to his post, conservative commentator Megyn Kelly simply wrote “Just stop” on her X account. There was no rush by any of Trump’s Cabinet members to endorse his claims.
But the conspiracy mill has been quietly grinding away over the past week.
One set of charts developed by Covid lockdown critic Kevin Bass claims that “Democrats materialized 20 million new votes” in 2026 compared to 2022. Trump amplified Bass’s claims via Truth Social on Sunday, and perhaps by Monday morning had convinced himself of their veracity.
The President’s former spokesperson, Liz Harrington, added fuel to the fire by suggesting Democrats had “over cheated” and accidentally revealed the scale of their fraud. There is not a scintilla of evidence to support those claims, and, problematically for the conspiracy theorists, Trump himself has repeatedly attributed his midterm loss to weak Republican candidates and soaring fuel prices.
Whether he is indicating a genuine determination to try to fight the outcome of the midterms is unclear. But even as he was pressing “publish” on his social media post, Democrats victorious in last week’s election were descending on Capitol Hill for their official orientation, aimed at ensuring when they start work in early January, they will know their way around the corridors of power.

sources.news_title: Trump's Election Conspiracy Machine Roars Back to Life After Brief Moment of Acceptance
sources.text:
For a few days, Donald Trump appeared to be doing something unusual: accepting an election defeat without immediately claiming the vote was rigged.

Just days after projecting a willingness to move forward, Trump is once again questioning the legitimacy of an election — without producing evidence of the widespread wrongdoing his post suggests.

Trump reverses stance, alleges fraud in recent US midterm elections
Democratic Senate leader Schumer criticises Trump’s poll denialism, calling it an avoidable return to baseless claims.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Monday. “How could the Polls be so wrong???”
While Republicans questioned whether polls were once again underestimating their support, as they had in the 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential elections, the results ultimately went the other way.
Polls had largely pointed to a strong night for Democrats, with surveys suggesting the party was well positioned to take control of the House of Representatives and had a realistic chance of winning the Senate.
In fact, Pew Research released a report analysing pre-election polling data and found that the data understated the Democratic margin by at least 2 points in 23 of 27 races for governor and the US Senate.
Trump also alleged on Truth Social that some early voting ballot counts were so large that they made it impossible for Republicans to win. He provided no evidence of election fraud or wrongdoing. Over the past few days, the president has shared posts on Truth Social with graphs questioning voter turnout data.
The post marks Trump’s first explicit public challenge to the integrity of the overall midterm results since Democrats overwhelmingly won control of both chambers of Congress, in addition to a string of victories in traditionally Republican strongholds.
This latest remark comes a day after an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes, in which Trump appeared to accept the election outcome. Asked about his decision to congratulate Democrats, Trump confirmed that he had done so and said he was open to working with the incoming Democratic majority.
Shortly after the Democratic Party’s victory was announced, Trump congratulated them on a call with CBS News and later told Fox News that the party “did a good job”.

Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer responded to Trump’s latest remarks, saying the president’s “return to election denialism was inevitable”.
“He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure,” Schumer wrote on X.

sources.news_title: Trump questions midterm election results over "wrong" polls amid blue wave
sources.text:
President Donald Trump questioned the results of the 2026 midterm elections in a post on Truth Social on Monday, asking how the polls could have been “so wrong” as the Republican Party continued grappling with major losses in the House of Representatives and Senate. One expert Newsweek spoke with, however, defended the polls, saying they "underestimated magnitude but got the vector right."
Polls underestimated Democrats by several points in the midterms, shattering the narrative that Republicans are routinely underestimated. RealClearPolitics’ generic ballot average showed Democrats up 8.8 points over Republicans, but Democrats ended up winning by 13 points, according to data from The New York Times as of Monday morning, when some votes were yet to be counted.
That had major implications for both parties. Although Democrats were seen as favorites to flip control of the House, and the Senate was seen as competitive, Democrats are poised to win both chambers easily, with more than 250 seats in the House and at least 54 seats in the Senate, with several seats uncalled.
Read More on News
Trump on Monday took to Truth Social, questioning if anyone believes the election was “honest.”
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” he wrote.
During a news conference later Monday, Trump was asked by a reporter if he believes the midterms “were rigged.”
“Well, I think the numbers were terrible in terms of those early votes. You look at all those early votes,” he said.
Polling error may come down to the estimates of who is considered a “likely voter,” a group that has been changing, Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek.
“In defense of the polls, they did correctly show and predict that races one would have thought would not be particularly competitive were in fact extremely competitive,” he said. “They underestimated magnitude but got the vector right. And there may have been some late-breaking voters, in terms of turnout and in terms of vote choice, who the polls simply missed through no fault of their own.”
As for future elections, Reeher said he believes Republicans still have around 43 percent of the vote “baked in.”
“Unless they field a really bad candidate, a presidential election year should generate its own enthusiasm,” he said. “And a lot depends of course on what Democrats do with this victory, in terms of their presidential own sweepstakes.”
Newsweek reached out to the Democratic and Republican national committees for comment via email.
How Wrong Were Polls in Key Senate Races?
Polling across the board underestimated Democrats in key Senate races.
The largest polling miss was in Texas, where polling showed Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico with a slight edge over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton—but Talarico ended up winning by double digits.
RCP’s average gave Talarico a 2.6-point lead, but he won by 12.1 points—a polling miss of more than 9 points.
Georgia also saw a 9-point polling miss. Senator Jon Ossoff led by an average of 8.4 points, per RCP, but was on track to win by 18 points.
In South Carolina, polling gave Senator Darline Graham a 2.6-point lead, but she was on track to lose to Democratic Senator-elect Annie Andrews by 4.5 points.
Here is a look at how polls missed in 11 key Senate races.
Republicans Banked on Pro-GOP Polling Error
In the final stretch of the campaign, Republicans said they believed polling was inaccurate and were banking on a pro-Republican polling error.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said during an interview on Fox News’ The Ingraham Angle that polls were “grossly underestimating Republican enthusiasm.”
“I think it’s even further off this time because more and more Republicans are unwilling to participate in these surveys. They don’t want to give their information to someone on the phone. They don’t play along. They’re calling it the partisan nonresponse bias,” he said.
Nate Silver wrote in an October 20 Substack post that pollsters are “acutely aware” of the challenge that Republicans are less likely to participate in polls and have a “variety of tactics and techniques to combat it.”
“They can match to Census Bureau demographics, or they can anchor to the past reported vote. Or there might be approaches that are a little bit more subjective: for instance, playing around with assumptions in likely voter models. Pollsters might herd or refuse to publish results they deem too far out of consensus; it’s happened before in the U.S. and abroad,” he wrote.
Polling Hasn’t Always Underestimated Republicans
While it is true that Republicans have been underestimated in polls during several recent elections, that is not always the case. Polling error is not replicated from cycle to cycle. Pro-Republican polling errors have been most pronounced during presidential years when Trump was on the ballot.
In 2018, the generic ballot polling error also favored Democrats, though by a less dramatic margin. RCP had Democrats up 7.3 points in their final average; they ended up winning by 8.4 points.
Polling was fairly accurate in 2022. Republicans led the generic ballot by 2.5 points, according to RCP, and went on to win by 2.8 points.
Republicans have modestly overperformed their polling in recent presidential races, though the difference has only been a few points.
In 2024, polling was only a few points off. RCP’s average had former Vice President Kamala Harris up only 0.1 points over Trump, who carried the national popular vote by 1.5 points.
In 2020, RCP had former President Joe Biden up 7.2 points in the polls; he ended up winning by 4.5 points, and by even narrower margins in key swing states. RCP had former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton up 3.2 points in 2016. She ended up winning the popular vote by just over 2 points, while losing the Electoral College.
What Has Donald Trump Said About Midterm Results?
Trump's latest comments mark a shift from his response on election night.
“I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” Trump told the New York Times on election night. “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out.”
In other election-night remarks, Trump sought to distance himself from the Republican defeat, writing on Truth Social: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”
Prior to the midterms, the president told reporters he would accept the results if they were "honest elections."
On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the U.S. "took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election."

sources.news_title: Trump Casts Doubt on Midterm Election Results
sources.text:
President Donald Trump questioned the integrity of the midterm elections on Monday, less than a week after the Republican Party suffered historic defeats in both swing states and former GOP strongholds.
“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump asked in a Truth Social post early Monday. “How could the Polls be so wrong???”
“Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” he continued, adding: “It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” His post did not elaborate on what was meant by the statement.
Read more: Welcome to Trump’s Lame-Duck Era
Trump’s unsubstantiated fraud claims come nearly two weeks after he told reporters on Oct. 27 that he would respect the election results “if they’re honest elections.”
As results came in throughout Nov. 3 and into Nov. 4, Trump seemed to accept the outcome.
“My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country,” Trump told CBS News in an election-night phone call.
It was a sentiment he repeated in an interview that aired Sunday on 60 Minutes, when he said he would be willing to work with Democrats on immigration, addressing an issue that had been top-of-mind for voters ahead of Election Day. “I think that's something that's actually doable," he said.
By Monday morning, however, Trump was casting doubt on the results. The comment harkens back to Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of election interference and ensuing lawsuits after he lost the presidency to Joe Biden in 2020.
Trump's history of election denial
Trump was sowing doubt on the 2020 election before voting began, telling the public that August that “the only way we’re going to lose this election is if the election is rigged.”
Following his loss, Trump refused to concede to Biden. Instead, he began to spread conspiracy theories about widespread election fraud, without evidence.
On Nov. 7, 2020, shortly before news organizations projected Biden’s victory, Trump falsely declared on Twitter that he had “WON THIS ELECTION, BY A LOT!”
Echoing Trump’s false claims also became a test of loyalty within the Republican Party, with House Speaker Mike Johnson, Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, and former Georgia Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene among those who espoused the false view.
Trump and his allies filed 62 lawsuits challenging or seeking to overturn the results between Nov. 4, 2020, and Jan. 6, 2021, according to the House Jan. 6 committee. Only one produced a victory—a narrow Pennsylvania ruling that didn’t establish fraud or change the outcome. Some cases were dismissed on procedural grounds; others failed on the merits.
The legal defeats did not stop Trump from repeating his false claims.
On Dec. 22, 2020, he alleged on social media that Democrats had “DUMPED HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF BALLOTS IN THE SWING STATES LATE IN THE EVENING.”
The claims escalated on Jan. 5, 2021, when Trump tweeted: “Washington is being inundated with people who don’t want to see an election victory stolen by emboldened Radical Left Democrats.”
This followed repeated calls for his supporters to descend upon Washington D.C. and protest the results.
As Congress met to count and certify the Electoral College votes on Jan. 6, 2021, a mob of Trump supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol.
His efforts to overturn his 2020 defeat also led to criminal charges. In August 2023, Special Counsel Jack Smith brought four federal charges against Trump, alleging efforts to subvert the results through pressure on officials, fraudulent elector slates, and interference with certification. Trump pleaded not guilty.
On the campaign trail in 2024, he doubled down on his allegations of election interference by urging voters to deliver a victory that was “too big to rig.”
The case was dismissed in November that year, after his reelection, because of Justice Department policy against prosecuting a sitting President.

Trump initially struck an unusually conciliatory tone, congratulating his opponents and acknowledging they had fought a successful campaign. “I am absolutely willing to accept those results,” he told The New York Times on election night, adding that he looked forward to working with Democrats. I really do.” But on Thursday, Trump demanded that votes cast for two minor candidates in Alaska’s still-undecided US Senate election be transferred to the trailing Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan. “There is no other fair solution!” he insisted, despite Alaska’s election laws providing for ranked-choice voting. Monday’s accusations went further, casting doubt on the legitimacy of the elections nationwide. They echoed Trump’s repeated and unfounded claims that the 2020 presidential election had been stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden. His refusal to accept that defeat sparked dozens of unsuccessful legal challenges and culminated in the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol by his supporters. ‘Election denialism’ Democrats reacted furiously to the president’s latest accusations. “Donald Trump’s pathetic return to election denialism was inevitable,” Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said. “He can whine all he wants, but nothing will stop this inescapable truth: For the last two years of his presidency, Trump will face the largest Democratic congressional majorities in decades, all because he has been an unprecedented failure.” Trump offered no details of the supposed irregularities, identifying neither the voting machines he questioned nor specific evidence that ballots had been improperly counted. sources.text:
Trump questions midterm elections integrity after previously accepting results
US President Donald Trump has questioned the legitimacy of the midterm election results in which Republicans suffered sweeping losses, days after saying he would accept the outcome.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
This appeared to contradict what he told the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results.
Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. State and local officials across the US said voting had been mostly problem-free.
Some key races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi, have yet to be called.
In the Truth Social post, Trump made vague claims about polling, voting "dumps", and "machines" without providing specific evidence of what this referred to and whether he believed there had been error or wrongdoing.
The reporting of vote counts on election night proceeded as normal, according to Charles Stewart III, a political scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
"We saw across the nation the standard patterns we see in terms of when the votes are reported," he said.
Stewart added that in some states, like Florida and Georgia, some initial reporting of results happens quickly because they already have the results of early and mail ballots.
Trump has previously attempted to cast doubts on the integrity of elections he has lost, although he himself was not on the ballot in the midterms.
"We would have won easily if I was on the ballot," Trump told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, after it was confirmed his party had lost both the Senate and the House.
Surveys ahead of the election from several pollsters and news outlets suggested that Republicans could lose seats in both the House and Senate.
As it stands, Democrats have won 54 US Senate seats and 254 US House seats in the midterms, giving them comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress even as counting continues in some races, like in Alaska and Mississippi.
"State laws and practicalities are such that some states will just take longer to count," said Ruth Greenwood, director of the Election Law Clinic at Harvard Law School.
"That doesn't mean anything nefarious is occurring—we just need to trust local election officials to count every vote and tell us the results when they are done."
The outcome has been clear since election night. Trump told the New York Times then: "We'll, you know, look forward to working with [Democrats]", adding: "We'll probably work something out."
He has also offered his own analysis of why Republicans lost, acknowledging on Fox News that the Iran war had contributed to the defeat.
"People agree with what I'm doing on Iran but they really probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline - I understand that," he said.
Vice-President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war, which began in February and which has severely disrupted global oil and gas supplies - causing costs to soar, as the reason their party lost the election.
In the run-up to the midterms, Trump made claims about widespread voting fraud, despite evidence that it is rare.
He and his allies alleged for months that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to former President Joe Biden, had been rigged against him. His lawyers and allies spent weeks attempting to litigate the results, but courts repeatedly struck them down.
The justice department during his administration has made unprecedented attempts to exert more federal control over elections - a power the Constitution primarily delegates to individual states.
Days before these midterms, it filed controversial lawsuits in federal courts challenging the count and certification of votes in states like California and Alaska, but judges ruled against them in nearly all instances.
Election law experts, state officials, and local elections offices told the BBC they had spent months preparing for a scenario in which the White House or election sceptics questioned the votes' legitimacy.
Despite the intense focus around election integrity on both sides of the debate, top state and local election officials have reported a mostly smooth process so far for the 2026 midterms.
Extreme weather did force some location closures, and a handful of reported administrative or technical issues slowed the process in some local jurisdictions.

"It's all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!" he added, signing off as "President DJT."
His remarks revived his practice of questioning electoral outcomes involving losses suffered by him and other Republican candidates. Trump announced last week that Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as top aide.
Trump’s latest missive represents a shift in the president’s outlook on the election results. Democrats materialized 20 million new votes.” A bar chart paired with the post compared House popular-vote numbers from 2022 with projections for 2026. Republicans were listed at 54.2 million votes two years earlier and a projected 55.6 million this cycle, while Democrats appeared at 51.3 million in 2022 and a projected 70.4 million now.
